subtype: Approach: pre-mortem with the whole team [Thinking]
passage:
Day 1, the evening before kickoff. Bidisha handed out paper and said, "Picture the launch having flopped half a year from now. Write down why." Even the quietest teammate filled a full page.

Day 2. Bidisha read the pages aloud without names. Two reasons topped the list: requirements nobody had pinned down, and a key person leaving. Hrithik, who owned the payment module, shifted in his chair. Bidisha said, "That's not blame, that's a plan. Let's make the requirements a signed page, and let a second person shadow the payment work."

Day 40. The client changed a screen, and the signed page settled it in a day. A week later Hrithik mentioned a job offer, and the shadow already knew the module.

qa.q: Which two reasons topped the list of possible failures?
qa.a: The two reasons were requirements nobody had pinned down and a key person leaving.

qa.q: What might Hrithik have felt when a key person leaving was named?
qa.a: Hrithik probably felt uneasy and exposed at first, since Hrithik owned the payment module, though Bidisha treated it as a plan rather than blame.

qa.q: What else could Bidisha do with the list, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha could review it again each month and cross off risks that have been handled, because risks change as the project moves.

qa.q: How might quieter teammates see the exercise?
qa.a: Quieter teammates may feel more free to speak up, since imagining a failure asks for honesty rather than criticism of anyone.

grounding: Illustrates a lead running a pre-mortem, having the team write why the project failed, and adding early safeguards for the top risks.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem with the whole team [Thinking]
passage:
"Sachin, before your team starts on Monday, let me tell you what your Himani didi did on her first project, back when I was twenty-four.
The kickoff was in our tiny office. Before anyone opened a laptop, I handed out sticky notes and said, 'Imagine it's six months from now and this project has failed. Write down why.'
People laughed, then got quiet and wrote. We stuck them on the wall. Two reasons came up again and again: 'Nobody knew what the client actually wanted,' and 'Kiran left and nobody else knew the payment code.'
So we fixed both before we began. I set up a weekly call with the client to confirm requirements in writing. And I paired Kiran with Asha on the payment code from day one.
Four months later, Kiran did leave. Asha picked it up the same week. That wall of sticky notes saved us."

qa.q: What two reasons came up most often on the sticky notes?
qa.a: Nobody knowing what the client wanted, and Kiran leaving with nobody else knowing the payment code.

qa.q: How did the team seem to feel when asked to imagine failure?
qa.a: They laughed at first, then became quiet and serious, suggesting they felt uneasy but engaged.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Himani's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Pairing Asha with Kiran from day one was the turning point, because when Kiran left, the project didn't stall.

qa.q: How might Asha have felt when Kiran left?
qa.a: Asha may have felt some pressure but also ready and confident, having worked on the payment code from the start.

grounding: Shows a lead running a pre-mortem at kickoff, finding unclear requirements and a key person leaving as top risks and safeguarding both early.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem with the whole team [Thinking]
passage:
Wasim's first project as lead had a tight start: the client wanted kickoff on Monday, and two of his five team members were still finishing another release. He had one hour on Friday evening with everyone in the room, pizza going cold.
He handed out paper. "Quick exercise. It's six months from now. This project has failed badly. Write why."
Jaya, the tester, wrote first. Others followed. Wasim read them aloud. Four out of five said some version of "requirements kept changing". Three said, "Jaya left and nobody could test the integrations."
Jaya looked up. "I'm not planning to leave."
"I know," Wasim said. "But if you're sick for a month, same problem."
So before Monday he emailed the client asking for a signed requirements list and a weekly change review. And he booked Jaya to spend two hours a week teaching Rohan the integration tests.
The pizza was cold, but the plan was warmer.

qa.q: How many team members said requirements kept changing?
qa.a: Four out of five said so.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel when her name came up as a risk?
qa.a: Jaya felt a little surprised and defensive, saying she wasn't planning to leave.

qa.q: What else could Wasim do to guard against other risks from the exercise?
qa.a: He could revisit the list at the end of each month, adding new risks and checking the safeguards still work.

qa.q: How might the client see Wasim's request for a signed requirements list?
qa.a: The client may find it a bit formal at first, but likely appreciates clear agreement and fewer surprises later.

grounding: Shows a lead running a pre-mortem at kickoff where unclear requirements and one key person leaving top the list, and adding safeguards for both.
